name: Rosa Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What's a usual working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a wheel loader at West Vale, a large copper mine. I move broken rock into the crusher and keep the feed steady, because one bad bucket can jam the line. I'm experienced, though there are operators there with better hands than mine. I enjoy the machine and the pay; the long night roster steals evenings from my family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the pay support outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Idris and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. He repairs small engines from our garage on weekends, and I keep the bookings and parts list; that is family work, not another full wage. We have more than six months of expenses saved, and other mines are hiring within driving distance. I did a vocational certificate, and I use an AI assistant every day to sort my shift notes and his repair bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the loader crew the clever software has saved a little paperwork, and that's fine. I would still want the foreman to watch the crusher and keep apprentices beside an experienced operator. No one learns rock from a screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage and shifts look steady, and the garage bookings don't depend on AI. I enjoy using the assistant to turn messy parts notes into a list. I would miss the chance to learn more, but a quiet future suits our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my loader roster and use the assistant to tidy each end-of-shift note. I'd raise our savings transfer by fifty each pay day. In the first year I'd ask Idris to show our daughter Mina how to price a repair, if she is interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would be relieved to have time for the children and a job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach Mina at the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let her add the parts and labour on one invoice, then check it with Idris. A child should see what work costs before asking for a new tool. She might prefer football; I would not force it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI for bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it saves me an hour on Sunday. I check every price myself before it goes to a customer. The assistant is handy, but my name is on the invoice.

say: I would praise **shorter notes** while asking that apprentices still learn beside operators.
I would say **crusher checks** belong with the crew even when office forms become easier.
think: Our **mine wage** and garage bookings look steady, with savings behind the mortgage.
I would enjoy a little **saved time** without expecting a new machine to change my life.
do: Keep the **loader roster** and check each AI tidied shift note before filing.
Raise the **savings transfer** by fifty each pay day to grow the family cushion.
feel: **Calm** about the job and household bills.
S0.quote: The assistant is handy, but my name is on the invoice.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** saves paperwork time but leaves her own checks in place.
Her **family teaching** reflects pride in earned skill without pressuring her daughter to enter the trade.

steps.text: Keep operating the West Vale loader and checking shift notes
Raise the family savings transfer by fifty each pay day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that buying and scheduling may change before the loader does. I'd ask whether the mine can use those savings to offer more paid apprenticeships. A useful machine should earn its keep, and a young worker should still get a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn the new ordering screen, and there are other pits if my roster shrinks. Still, fewer people may be needed near the crusher as machines spread into physical work. Idris's garage could get more repair customers, but I wouldn't count that income before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask to try the mine's new stock-ordering screen with the stores clerk and learn it on a paid shift. In the first year I'd keep a written count of crusher stoppages and apply for loader work at another nearby mine if my shifts are cut. I'd ask the foreman to keep one apprentice on my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I like learning the screen, but I would hate to see the younger workers shut out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the stoppage count show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would show whether our crew actually keeps the crusher running better than a smaller crew. I want a crusher-stoppage count the foreman can check, not a speech. If my hours fall anyway, I would use that record in another job application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring Idris into this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my husband Idris that the garage must stand on its own figures. We would keep the savings account for the family, not buy extra tools because the mine looks uncertain. He agrees with me on that.

say: I would support **paid apprenticeships** if software cuts buying and scheduling costs.
I would tell the crew that **loader work** changes more slowly than office screens.
think: I could learn the **ordering screen**, but a smaller crusher crew could still reduce my hours.
I would treat **garage income** as uncertain until actual repair orders arrive.
do: Learn the **stock screen** with the stores clerk during a paid shift this month.
Record **crusher stoppages** and apply at nearby pits if my loader hours are cut.
feel: **Uneasy** about my roster and apprentices, despite practical options.
S1.quote: I want a crusher-stoppage count the foreman can check, not a speech.
fieldNote: She uses **operating evidence** to defend her role without assuming it guarantees a job.
Her **apprenticeship request** follows her values, while the family reserve stays separate from the garage.

steps.text: Learn the mine stock-ordering screen on a paid shift
Apply for nearby loader work if West Vale cuts shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could handle stock orders and crusher schedules almost at once. The card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031, so the loader is not replaced on the first date. I would ask for clear equipment plans and keep apprentices learning machines while they can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shift paperwork could disappear by 2028, and the loader wage could be in danger around 2031. The other pits might buy the same robots, so nearby vacancies are no guarantee. Idris can repair engines, but his weekend garage cannot carry the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the planned family holiday this month and move that money into a separate mortgage reserve. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for machine repair shifts at West Vale and ask Idris to show me the garage's common engine faults. I would also ask the equipment manager when a loader trial is actually funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would expect a large hit to our pay if the loader goes, and I would wake up thinking about the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new garage equipment now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not before the repair orders justify it. I am willing to try a new tool, but I will not borrow against the house on a guess. Idris and I can use what is already in the garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mina and Sami, our children, that we are keeping the holiday money at home for now. I would not say the mine is closing when we have no such news. We can still take a day trip together.

say: I would mark **2028 office changes** and the separate 2031 robot risk for the loader.
I would ask for **funded equipment plans** while keeping apprentices on real machines.
think: The **loader wage** could fall around 2031, and other mines may face the same pressure.
The **garage cannot** cover the family mortgage on its weekend orders alone.
do: Cancel the **family holiday** and move its budget into a mortgage reserve this month.
Apply for **machine repair** shifts after 2028 and learn common engine faults with Idris.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely major wage hit and the mortgage.
S2.quote: I will not borrow against the house on a guess.
fieldNote: Her **fast response** protects mortgage cash before any robot arrives.
She seeks **repair work** rather than assuming the small garage can replace mine income.
Her **equipment caution** limits risk despite her comfort with new technology.

steps.text: Cancel the planned family holiday this month
Apply for machine repair shifts at West Vale after 2028
Learn common engine faults beside Idris in the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI by 2031 leaves time to learn a second machine. The planning and ordering work may change in 2031, while capable hands-on robots arrive around 2034. I would ask the mine to offer real repair apprenticeships before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the thinking system arrives and 51 at the robot date. Five years could let me qualify for maintenance, though that job might change too. The family reserve would let us choose a course without selling the house, but I would still need wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the mine's maintenance certificate this year if there is a funded place, and take a night module otherwise. I'd keep my loader shifts while learning and send each overtime payment to the mortgage. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for a maintenance vacancy if one exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the timetable gives me a usable route. I cannot treat a certificate as a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from a funded place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid hours and time beside a fitter, not just videos at home. I would bring my loader experience to the workshop, but I need to learn how to trace faults. If the mine does not fund it, I will take one evening module myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the garage become your main work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the bookings and prices support two steady incomes, which they do not today. Idris and I can grow it slowly. I will keep the mine wage as long as the shifts exist.

say: I would ask for **repair apprenticeships** before 2034, when capable hands-on robots arrive on the card.
I would explain that **2031 planning changes** give operators a few years to gain workshop skills.
think: A **maintenance qualification** offers a possible move, not a promised replacement wage.
Our **family reserve** buys course time, but the mortgage still needs a regular payment.
do: Enroll in **maintenance training** this year, using a funded place or an evening module.
Send **earned overtime** to the mortgage and apply for a vacancy after 2031 if available.
feel: **Anxious**, with a workable but uncertain route to another paid role.
S3.quote: I cannot treat a certificate as a job offer.
fieldNote: She states a **funding condition** yet commits to an evening module if the mine declines.
The **garage remains supplemental** until real bookings can support a second full income.

steps.text: Enroll in a funded maintenance course or evening module this year
Send each earned overtime payment to the family mortgage
Apply for a West Vale maintenance vacancy after 2031 if available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to build useful skills and businesses. Ordering may change in 2036, while hands-on robots arrive around 2039 on the card. I would encourage the mine to keep apprenticeships open and publish equipment plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, with the children older and, if our payments hold, less mortgage left. I might be running a repair shop with Idris by then, but only if customers make it viable. Even good repair work could face robots after 2039, so I cannot call it safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take a paid short course on loader hydraulics and spend one evening a week on garage repairs with Idris. I'd keep the mine job and make our scheduled mortgage payments. In the first year after 2036 I'd review actual garage takings before considering shorter mine hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not rushed. A decade lets us test the garage without staking the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the garage can support shorter shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need a full year of steady bookings after parts and tax, not a busy month. I would write down that number with Idris before asking for fewer mine shifts. My children need stable meals, not my enthusiasm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices at West Vale to learn the machines inside and out and keep records of what they fix. The tools will change, but paid experience matters. I would also tell them to keep some money aside.

say: I would ask the mine for **equipment plans** and continued apprenticeships through the 2036 and 2039 changes.
I would tell younger workers that **paid experience** and saved money give them more choices.
think: The **garage could grow** over ten years if actual repair demand holds up.
I cannot assume **repair work** stays secure after the hands-on robot date around 2039.
do: Take a **hydraulics course** and practise garage repairs with Idris one evening weekly.
Keep **mine shifts** and review a full year of garage takings after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy** about the eventual robot risk, with time to test another income.
S4.quote: My children need stable meals, not my enthusiasm.
fieldNote: She makes **garage growth conditional** on a full year of net takings.
Her **traditional family concern** tempers a genuine interest in new tools and business.

steps.text: Take a paid loader hydraulics course this year
Keep operating the West Vale loader on regular shifts
Review a full year of garage takings after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the loader wage and garage could both be squeezed before we have much time. I would want an honest equipment timetable and paid entry into machine repair, not a promise of a job that is not there. Our savings help, but a household still needs work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches the next group of operators if the mine stops taking apprentices. I learned beside people who corrected me before I broke a machine. I would like my children to see that kind of learning still exists.

headlineQuote: Our savings help, but a household still needs work.
portrait: **Rosa Ibrahim**, 43, runs a wheel loader at a large copper mine and helps her husband manage weekend engine repairs.
Her **mine wage** supports a mortgage and two school-age children, while savings and nearby pits offer more than one option.
She uses **AI daily** for notes and bookings, yet insists apprentices learn with experienced workers beside real equipment.
Fast AGI threatens **both incomes**; slower timelines let her test maintenance skills and garage demand without gambling the house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could put her loader wage and the family garage under pressure before she has much time.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest equipment timetable** and paid entry to machine repair would help her plan a real move.
